data.query_text: How did I fix the Postgres deadlock?
data.answer:
You fixed it by making every transaction take its row locks in the same order. The deadlock came from two workers upserting the same rows in different orders [Memory 1]. You sorted each batch by primary key before the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`, cut the batch size from 5000 to 500, and added a retry on SQLSTATE `40P01` with jitter, three attempts at most [Memory 2].

Your notes on the book chapter explain why the retry is still needed: the database breaks a lock cycle by aborting one transaction, and the application has to run it again [Memory 3].

sources.excerpt:
[ASSISTANT]
The deadlock comes from two transactions upserting the same set of rows in a different order\. Each takes a row lock the other needs. Sort the batch by primary key before the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT so every transaction acquires its locks in the same order.

[USER]
Sorting fixed it in staging. I also dropped the batch size from 5000 to 500 and added a retry on SQLSTATE 40P01 with jitter, three attempts max. My pick\: keep the retry even if the sort holds up.

Deadlocks arise when transactions wait on each other in a cycle. The database detects the cycle and aborts one of them so that the others can make progress; the aborted transaction must be retried by the application.

[CLAUDE]
For the migration, take an advisory lock first so only one worker runs it. pg_advisory_xact_lock releases at commit, which is what you want here.

data.query_text: What was the trick for keeping the Docker layer cache warm?
data.answer: Install dependencies before you copy the source. Your notes say the lockfile changes rarely, so the dependency layer stays cached and only the final copy and build re-run [Memory 1]. You also pinned the base image by digest so a new upstream tag would not invalidate everything [Memory 2].

sources.excerpt: Order the Dockerfile so dependency installation comes before copying the source. The lockfile changes rarely, so that layer stays cached.
Pin the base image by digest, not by tag. A moving tag silently busts every layer above it.

data.query_text: why does faiss recall drop after I delete documents
data.answer: Because the index was rebuilt and the row numbers shifted while your code still used the old ones. The conversation concludes that a flat index has no in-place delete, so every delete rebuilds it, and any stored row id goes stale [Memory 1]. The fix you settled on was to keep a separate list that maps each row to a chunk id and rebuild that list together with the index.

sources.source: Why is my FAISS recall dropping after deletes
sources.excerpt:
[ASSISTANT]
IndexFlatIP cannot remove vectors in place. If you rebuild it without the deleted rows, every later row moves up, so any row number you stored earlier now points at a different vector.

sources.excerpt:
[ASSISTANT]
A future has to own or outlive everything it touches across an await point, because it may be moved to another thread and resumed later. A borrow of a local that ends before the await is fine; one that spans it is not.
